claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist in a simple solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution may contain varying degrees of order or segregation.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable plasticity.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable machinability.
Composition can alter solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Processing history or thermal treatment can alter solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Composition, processing history, or thermal treatment can promote or suppress nanoscale precipitates or clusters in CoCrFeNiTi.
The interplay of solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and nanoscale precipitates or clusters governs deformation behavior in CoCrFeNiTi.
The interplay of solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and nanoscale precipitates or clusters governs hardness and strength in CoCrFeNiTi.
Changing composition, processing history, or thermal treatment will alter deformation behavior, hardness, and strength relative to the starting alloy.
Suitable changes may improve hardness and strength while maintaining favorable plasticity and machinability.
The hypothesis is restricted to compressive loading at temperatures up to 600 °C.
The permitted interventions do not alter the alloy's fundamental solid-solution state.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires interventions not to alter the fundamental solid-solution state, while the proposed mediator and intervention invoke formation of nanoscale precipitates, which may constitute a phase or state change. No criterion distinguishes permissible clusters from precipitates that violate the boundary.
